title: Pass on only answers that can be checked

blocks.text: The network now signs its answers, with a MAC key it shares with us (`zak.network`). The terminals check ours, each under its own key (`tak.` plus its terminal ID). Since the change, the terminals' support line hears two complaints: some of our answers fail the terminal's check, and the network team asks why we passed on an answer of theirs that someone had changed on the way.

`src/main/java/com/example/practice/NetworkAnswers.java` holds two participants. `CheckNetworkMac` stands right after `QueryHost`; `SignForTerminal` stands right before `SendResponse`. Between them, an abort participant answers `91` when it finds no response in the Context. Finish the parts marked `TODO`. `mac(message, key)` and `key(alias)` are given. About fifteen lines in total.

The tests deploy a real TransactionManager, `QueryHost` and QMUX in the test's own JVM, with a real software security module. The network on the far side signs, declines, or sends answers that are not what it signed.

cases.says: the network's approval reaches each terminal with a MAC that verifies under that terminal's own key
the network's decline reaches the terminal as a decline it can check
an answer that fails the network's MAC is not passed on; the terminal gets 91 instead
an answer that carries no MAC from the network is treated like one with a wrong MAC
a decline the server makes itself on the abort path also reaches the terminal signed

origin.section: 7.4 Every Response Is Signed, on the Abort Path Too

concepts: Every answer is signed under its terminal's key by an abort participant right before SendResponse; an unsigned decline is an unknown outcome to the terminal, and a network answer is believed only when its own MAC verifies.
